prompt.context: SuperTech is an electronics retailer in India. Over the past few years, SuperTech has experienced a decrease in profitability and has engaged us to identify the causes and possible solutions.
prompt.question: Identify the causes of SuperTech's declining profitability and recommend possible solutions.

clarifying_info.a: No, this is not an industry-wide issue.

clarifying_info.q: Does SuperTech operate in multiple countries?
clarifying_info.a: No, the company only operates in India.

clarifying_info.q: Has there been a change in the mix of product offerings?
clarifying_info.a: No, there has been no change in their mix of product offerings.
No, SuperTech is not vertically integrated; they are a retailer of third-party products.

exhibits.title: SuperTech Electronics Financial Summary ($000s)
exhibits.shows: A table showing Revenue, Costs (COGS), SG&A, Margin, and Margin/Revenue (%) for the years 2011, 2012, and 2013. The Margin and Margin/Rev rows are left blank for the candidate to complete.

exhibits.title: Cell Phone Stock Out Days 2013
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the number of cell phone stock-out days per month in 2013, plotted for each month January through December. Values vary by month and appear elevated in certain periods.

exhibits.title: Unit Contribution Margins and Total Revenue by Product Category
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing unit contribution margin percentages for Cell Phones, Cameras, Televisions, and Computers, with total revenue figures listed for each category.

framework: Revenue: examine price changes and volume changes by product category
Revenue drivers: store traffic, purchases by category, margin per product
Costs: split fixed (store locations, overhead, staff) vs. variable (COGS, inventory, transportation)
External factors: new competitors, competitor strategy shifts, changes in customer preferences, market demographics, product obsolescence, brand/reputation issues

questions.prompt: Question 1: What are some potential causes of the profitability decline you would want to explore?
questions.guidance: A strong answer brainstorms in a structured, MECE way covering: (1) Revenue side — price or volume changes, store traffic, purchases by category, product mix; (2) Cost side — fixed costs (store locations, overhead, staff) and variable costs (COGS, inventory, transportation, warehousing); (3) External factors — new competitors or competitor strategy changes, shifts in customer preferences or demographics, product obsolescence, brand or promotion issues. Note: Deloitte Round 1 typically skips framework-building time; candidate should brainstorm aloud in structured fashion.

questions.prompt: Question 2: What can you infer from Exhibit 1? Calculate gross margin for each year.
questions.guidance: Key inferences: (1) Revenue is increasing each year; (2) Costs (COGS) are increasing at a faster rate than revenue; (3) Gross margin is declining in both absolute dollars and as a percentage. Candidate should compute Margin = Revenue - Costs - SG&A and Margin/Rev for each year.

math.setup: Margin = Revenue - Costs - SG&A; Margin/Rev = Margin / Revenue
math.answer: Margins declined from 31% (2011) to 28% (2012) to 25.5% (2013), driven by COGS rising faster than revenue.

questions.prompt: Question 3: What do you think is driving the increase in costs?
questions.guidance: A strong answer brainstorms multiple cost drivers: increasing labor costs in a developing country; higher gas/transportation costs; warehousing and inventory-related costs; loss of negotiating power with suppliers; increases in raw material costs of products. Interviewer should probe for inventory costs if not mentioned, then transition to Question 4 once inventory is identified.

questions.prompt: Question 4: Given Exhibit 2 (stock-out data) and Exhibit 3 (contribution margins), quantify the financial impact of cell phone stock-outs in 2013.
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe: (1) Exhibit 2 shows stock-outs concentrated in summer and year-end months — suggesting seasonality; (2) Exhibit 3 shows cell phones have the highest contribution margin (~60%) making stock-outs particularly costly; (3) On average there are ~5 stock-out days per month (sum of monthly days / 12 months from exhibit ≈ 5), equivalent to 1/6 of the year. Candidate must ask for revenue or contribution figures; interviewer provides Exhibit 3. Then candidate quantifies the lost contribution.

math.setup: Average stock-out days per month ≈ 5; assume 360-day year => 5/6 of a year is operational, 1/6 is lost. Cell phone total revenue = $240M (from Exhibit 3). Lost revenue = $240M * (1/6). Lost contribution = Lost Revenue * 60% CM.
steps: Adjusted margin if no stock-outs: ($140M + $28.8M) / $550M = $168.8M / $550M ≈ 30.69% (round to ~31%)
Margin loss attributable to stock-outs: 30.69% - 25.5% ≈ 5.19 percentage points
math.answer: Stock-outs in cell phones cost approximately $28.8M in lost contribution in 2013, representing ~5 percentage points of margin erosion.

questions.prompt: Question 5: What would you tell the client? Are rising costs due to stock-outs only? What else would you want to know, and what initial recommendations do you have?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note: (1) Stock-outs explain ~5 pp of margin loss but are not the only driver — COGS are rising broadly; (2) Investigate whether stock-outs affect other product categories beyond cell phones; (3) Provide structured recommendations to reduce stock-outs.

brainstorming.prompt: What recommendations would you give the client to reduce cell phone stock-outs?

categories.name: Supplier contract changes
ideas: Add contract option for rush/emergency orders from suppliers during peak demand
Negotiate higher safety stock levels going into summer and year-end months

categories.name: Demand forecasting
ideas: Reassess sales demand forecasting models for seasonal peaks (summer and end of year)
Use historical stock-out data to build better replenishment triggers

categories.name: Promotions alignment
ideas: Adjust cell phone promotions to coincide with months when inventory is most reliably on hand
Avoid heavy promotions during months historically prone to stock-outs

categories.name: Supply chain operations
ideas: Review order lead times and identify bottlenecks causing late replenishment
Explore alternative or backup suppliers to reduce single-source dependency

recommendation: SuperTech's profitability decline is driven by COGS growing faster than revenue, with a significant ~$28.8M contribution loss (≈5 pp of margin) attributable to cell phone stock-outs in high-demand months
The client should prioritize fixing inventory management for its highest-margin category (cell phones) through improved demand forecasting and revised supplier contracts
risks: Stock-out issues may also affect other product categories — full impact could be larger than modeled
Supplier contract renegotiation may increase per-unit costs if suppliers gain leverage
Demand forecasting improvements require reliable historical data and analytical capability
next_steps: Audit stock-out frequency across all product categories to size the total inventory problem
Renegotiate supplier contracts to add rush-order options and adjust safety stock levels before the next peak season
Implement seasonal demand forecasting and align promotional calendar to inventory availability
Investigate other COGS drivers (labor, transportation, warehousing) to address the residual margin gap not explained by stock-outs
